summary: Jesus calls His disciples to be ready and faithful like servants awaiting their master, speaks of the fire and division He brings, and urges the crowds to read the times.
key_insight: The master in Jesus’ story does what no master was expected to do: he comes home, girds himself, seats his watching servants at the table, and waits on them. The reward for waiting on the Master is to be served by Him.
story: “Let your waist be girded and your lamps burning,” Jesus said. His disciples were to be like servants waiting for their master to come home from a wedding, ready to open the door the moment he knocked. “Blessed are those servants whom the master, when he comes, will find watching.” He would gird himself, have them sit down to eat, and come and serve them, whether he came in the second watch or the third.
A homeowner who knew the hour the thief was coming would stay awake. “Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.”

Peter asked, “Lord, do You speak this parable only to us, or to all people?” Jesus answered with a question: “Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his master will make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?” Blessed is the servant his master finds doing his work; he will be set over all his master has. But the servant who says to himself, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat the other servants and get drunk, will be caught unaware and cut in two.
The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it would be beaten with many stripes; the one who did not know, with few. “For everyone to whom much is given, from him much will be required.”

Then Jesus spoke of His own mission. “I came to send fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am till it is accomplished!” He had not come to bring peace on earth but division, even inside one house: father against son, mother against daughter, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law.

To the crowds He said that when they saw a cloud rising in the west, they said a shower was coming, and when the south wind blew, they expected heat. “Hypocrites! You can discern the face of the sky and of the earth, but how is it you do not discern this time?” A man on his way to court with his adversary should settle on the road, before the judge hands him to the officer and he is thrown into prison until he has paid “the very last mite.”

scene.label: Girded and lit
scene.text: Men wore long robes. To work, run or travel, they pulled the hem up and tucked it into the belt. Israel ate the first Passover dressed that way, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11). Clay oil lamps had to be refilled and trimmed to stay burning through the night.

scene.label: The night watches
scene.text: Jews divided the night into three watches, and Romans into four. Either way, the second and third watches meant the deep of the night, the hours when waiting servants were most likely to doze.

scene.label: Fire and a baptism
scene.text: John the Baptist had promised that the Coming One would baptize “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16). Jesus says He must first undergo a baptism Himself, the same picture He used for His suffering when James and John asked for thrones (Mark 10:38).

scene.label: Weather signs
scene.text: In Israel, clouds from the west come off the Mediterranean and bring rain; Elijah’s servant saw a cloud “rising out of the sea” before the storm broke (1 Kings 18:44). The south wind blows in from the desert and brings scorching heat. Farmers read these signs every day.

scene.label: The last mite
scene.text: The mite was the smallest copper coin in use, worth a tiny fraction of a day’s wage. A debtor could be jailed until every bit of the debt was paid. The time to settle was on the road, before reaching the judge.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke gathers these sayings here, right after the warning about greed: those who are not to hoard must instead be ready for the Master’s coming. Matthew records the thief and the faithful servant in the Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24:43–51) and the warning about division when Jesus sent out the Twelve (Matthew 10:34–36); Jesus likely used these pictures more than once. Luke alone has Peter’s question, the servant beaten with few stripes, and Jesus’ longing for His baptism to be accomplished.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Master who will return and judge His servants, and the Master who serves them. On His last night He would gird Himself with a towel and wash His disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), and He was already pressing toward the baptism of suffering that would make that service complete.
seeing.living: Readiness is not anxious guessing about dates; it is doing today what the Master gave you to do, especially for the people of His household. Much has been given to you, so much will be asked. Do not settle into the thought that He is delaying.
seeing.ponder: If the Master knocked tonight, would He find you at the door with your lamp burning?

preaching.big_idea: Serve faithfully while you wait; the Master who comes will serve His watching servants.
outline: A Lord who brings fire and division (49–53)
A time to read and respond (54–59)
preaching.watch_for: Peter’s question (v. 41) turns the passage. Jesus answers with a question of His own (v. 42) and moves from all servants waiting to stewards entrusted with others; the warnings grow sharper for those who know more (vv. 47–48).
